subject: English
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 7 periods = 280 minutes
Total: 7 periods · 4h 40min

periods.activity_title: Entering the Poem: Prayer, Feeling, and First Reading

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us read (p.52): which of three sentences is closest to a prayer — oral discussion.
Let us discuss (p.53): silent reading, underline agreed lines, share in groups.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads three sentences aloud from “Let us read” (p.52) and invites students to say which feels most like a prayer and why. A quick paired exchange gathers two or three responses before the class settles.

Teacher reads the full poem “A Friend’s Prayer” aloud at a measured pace while students follow in their books (p.52–53). Teacher reads a second time, modelling the tone of a quiet vow, then invites volunteers to read individual stanzas aloud.

Students read the poem silently and underline the lines they personally agree with, as directed in “Let us discuss” (p.53). Groups of three then share which lines they chose and explain their choices briefly.

Each group reports which single line was underlined by the most members, as the “Let us discuss” task on page 53 asks. Teacher draws out two or three lines for the whole class and notes the warmth in the poem’s tone.

periods.teacher_notes: The poem is written as a heartfelt prayer addressed to the idea of friendship itself, so students often respond to its earnest, devotional tone before they analyse it — let that personal engagement lead the first reading. The AABB rhyme scheme gives the poem a vow-like cadence; pointing this out while reading aloud helps students hear the prayer quality the pre-reading task asks them to identify. Students who are reluctant to share in groups may be encouraged with the observation that there is no wrong line to underline — personal connection is the point here.

periods.activity_title: Reading Closely: Summary, Stanzas, and the Speaker's Character

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.54): complete poem summary by circling correct words.
Let us think and reflect (p.54): read stanza 3 lines, answer three questions.
Let us think and reflect (p.55): read stanzas 4–5 lines, answer three questions.

homework.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.54): answer in one word — how the poet feels about special friends, and what she uses to understand them.

time_bands.activity: Teacher projects or reads the summary cloze from “Let us discuss” (p.54) aloud, pausing at each highlighted word pair. Students circle their choice individually, then compare with a partner before the class agrees on each answer.

Teacher reads stanza 3 aloud (“I want to do much more than share”), then works through the three questions in “Let us think and reflect” (p.54) with the class: character choice, how wishes come true, and the fill-in sentence. Students respond orally first, then write the fill-in answer.

Teacher reads stanzas 4–5 aloud (“Let me use my heart to see”), then takes the three questions from “Let us think and reflect” (p.55): the line about feelings, character choice, and the fill-in blank on judgements. Students write answers; teacher confirms with the class.
Teacher sets the one-word answer task from “Let us discuss” (p.54) as an at-home task, reminding students to look back at the poem before writing.

periods.teacher_notes: The summary cloze on page 54 is a reliable check of whether students have read the whole poem carefully — the distinctions between ‘prayer for’ and ‘speech on’, or ‘heart’ and ‘mind’, mirror the poem’s central imagery. A common difficulty is the MCQ on stanza 3: students may choose ‘clever’ because the speaker seems to plan carefully; draw attention to the word ‘care’ in the stanza to redirect them. The poem’s most striking image — ‘Let me use my heart to see’ — is the heart as an organ of understanding, not mere emotion; a brief discussion of this repays the time spent.

periods.activity_title: Reflecting on the Prayer and Listening to Two Friends

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.55): give one reason this poem is a prayer.
Let us think and reflect (p.55): why does the speaker want to do more for her friend?
Let us listen (p.56): listen to outdoor-activities talk, answer in one or two words.
Let us listen (p.56): listen again, circle pictures matching activities described.

time_bands.activity: Teacher poses the two reflective questions from “Let us think and reflect” (p.55): why the poem counts as a prayer, and why the speaker wants to do more. Students think independently for a moment, then share answers in pairs before the teacher consolidates two or three responses — drawing on the poem’s AABB vow-like cadence and the speaker’s selfless devotion.

Teacher reads the listening transcript aloud at a natural conversational pace — a talk about the outdoor activities of Ajay and Dhiraj — while students listen with books closed. Students then write a one-or-two word answer to the first question in “Let us listen” (p.56).

Teacher reads the transcript a second time while students look at the six pictures in “Let us listen” (p.56) and circle those that match the activities described. Teacher then reviews answers with the class, naming each activity from the transcript to confirm.

Brief whole-class check: teacher asks students to name one activity from the transcript they personally enjoy with a friend, making a short bridge between the listening content and the poem’s theme of shared friendship.

periods.teacher_notes: The reflective questions on page 55 ask students to reason about genre (what makes something a prayer) and about the speaker’s motivation — both draw on the poem’s dominant theme of selfless devotion, which the poem appreciation describes as the speaker wishing to actively work to make friends’ wishes come true. For the listening task, read the transcript steadily and without dramatic pauses; the six-picture task on page 56 requires students to discriminate among similar leisure activities, so a second reading at normal speed is more useful than a slow one. Students sometimes circle the ‘reading on mat’ picture rather than the ‘park bench reading’ picture — steer them back to the transcript’s specific wording.

periods.activity_title: Speaking as Friends: Guided Role-Play Conversations

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us speak (p.57): role-play two friend situations in pairs — park walk and tiffin sharing.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads both role-play situations from “Let us speak” (p.57) aloud so students understand the structure: each conversation begins with a greeting, moves through a shared activity plan or food exchange, and closes with appreciation. Teacher models a short opening exchange for situation 1 with a volunteer.

Pairs work through situation 1 (a walk in the park): they greet, negotiate the park visit, plan activities together or propose an alternative, and share what they enjoy doing together. Teacher circulates, prompting pairs who are silent with the cue prompts on page 57.

Pairs switch roles and work through situation 2 (sharing tiffins at school): they greet, name their tiffin items, invite sharing, express how it feels, appreciate the food, and thank each other. Two or three pairs are invited to perform their conversation briefly for the class.

Class reflection: teacher asks what language they used to appreciate a friend and to thank them, collecting two or three expressions on the board. Students note one expression they found natural and one they found difficult.

periods.teacher_notes: The role-play situations on page 57 are deliberately low-stakes — familiar settings of park visits and school tiffins — so hesitant speakers can manage without losing confidence; encourage students who tend not to initiate to take the role of the friend who suggests the park visit. A common difficulty is students defaulting to very short answers (‘Yes, let us go’) without elaborating; the task sheet prompts them to plan activities and share feelings, so redirect them to those prompts if exchanges stall. The appreciation and thanks sub-task at the end of situation 2 is the most linguistically rich part and deserves the unhurried time the performing pairs get.

periods.activity_title: Writing About Friendship: Planning, Drafting, and Sharing

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write (p.57): list When/Where/How details about a friendship, then write an 80-word paragraph with a title.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the writing task from “Let us write” (p.57) aloud and explains the three-step structure: first list answers to When, Where, and How the friendship started; then build sentences from the list; then shape those sentences into a paragraph of about 80 words with a title. Teacher shows what a bare list looks like compared with full sentences using a brief example on the board.

Students work individually to list their When, Where, and How answers in their notebooks. Teacher circulates and prompts students who are stuck with questions such as “where did you first meet this friend?” or “what did you first do together?”

Students write their paragraph of about 80 words, using their list as a guide. Teacher circulates, checking that students are forming complete sentences and not simply copying the list. Students also choose and write a title for their paragraph.

Three or four volunteers read their paragraphs aloud to the class. Teacher invites one peer comment per reading — what detail they found most vivid or surprising — then guides students to check their own paragraph for a title and to count approximately 80 words.

periods.teacher_notes: The task on page 57 moves through planning to drafting in a single sitting, which is appropriate for an 80-word paragraph; students who treat the list step as optional tend to produce thin paragraphs, so ensure everyone fills in all three columns before writing. A common difficulty is students writing about their best friend in general rather than about how the friendship started — redirect them to the specific When, Where, How frame. The poem’s opening lines (‘May my friendships always be / The most important thing to me’) can serve as a brief motivating touchstone before students begin.

periods.activity_title: Words for Friendship: Meanings, Qualities, and Sentences

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.55): select words similar in meaning to 'blessed' from a given list.
Let us learn (p.55–56): complete partial words for friendship qualities and fill five blanks.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the line ‘With special friends I feel I’m blessed’ from the poem aloud and asks students what ‘blessed’ feels like. The class then works through the synonym-selection task in “Let us learn” (p.55), discussing each option — ‘excited’, ‘grateful’, ‘understood’, ‘thankful’, ‘relaxed’ — and deciding which ones are close in meaning to ‘blessed’ in the context of friendship.

Students work individually to complete the five partial words for friendship qualities (loyal, helpful, kind, caring, honest) in the word-building section of “Let us learn” (p.55–56). Teacher reveals the completed words one by one and discusses what each quality means.

Students fill in the five blank sentences in “Let us learn” (p.56) using the five friendship-quality words. Teacher reviews answers sentence by sentence, asking volunteers to read their completed sentence aloud and to explain why that quality fits the description given.

Quick consolidation: teacher asks students to say which of the five qualities they think the speaker in the poem shows most clearly, pointing to a line as evidence. One or two quick responses close the unit.

periods.teacher_notes: The synonym task for ‘blessed’ is drawn directly from the poem’s second stanza, so students should have the poem open; the distinction between ‘grateful’ and ‘thankful’ (both correct) and ‘excited’ (incorrect) is worth a brief class discussion. The word-building step — completing the partial words — is meant to help students notice the spelling of ‘helpful’ and ‘honest’ before using them in sentences; do not skip it by simply telling students the words. Students who finish the fill-in task early can be directed to the open-ended task on page 56 (writing three sentences about three friends) as a self-study extension.

periods.activity_title: Friendship Quotations: Meaning, Experience, and a Decorated Display

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us explore (p.58): discuss meaning of two friendship quotations and share a personal experience.
Let us explore (p.58): write, colour, and decorate a friendship quotation for the class board.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the two friendship quotations from “Let us explore” (p.58) aloud: ‘A friend in need is a friend indeed’ and ‘My best friend is the one who brings out the best in me.’ Students share what they think each quotation means; teacher guides the class to unpack the key ideas.

Students think of a personal experience that fits one of the two quotations and share it briefly with a partner, then two or three students share with the whole class. Teacher links the shared experiences back to the poem’s idea of unconditional acceptance and actively making friends’ wishes come true.

Students choose any friendship quotation — from the textbook or one they know in any language — and write it neatly on a piece of paper, then colour and decorate it for the class board, as directed in “Let us explore” (p.58). Teacher circulates, helping students who cannot recall a quotation by suggesting the two from the textbook.
Completed quotation cards are placed on the class board. Teacher invites a quick gallery walk of two minutes, after which one or two students name a card that caught their eye and explain why.

periods.teacher_notes: The two quotations on page 58 have different emphases — one is about loyalty under difficulty, the other about mutual growth — so it is worth asking students which they find more important and why, rather than treating them as equivalent. The decorating activity is genuinely creative and produces a physical class display, so ensure drawing materials are available; students who cannot recall a quotation in English may offer one in their home language, which the task explicitly allows. The personal-experience sharing step can surface shy speakers if the teacher first models a brief, low-stakes story of her own.

items.source_lo: Student identifies and interprets the speaker's feelings, intentions, and values using a lyric poem as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Selfless devotion, unconditional acceptance, empathy as basis of friendship; AABB prayer-cadence poem by Jill Wolf.
items.item_stem: Read the lines beginning "Let me use my heart to see" in Jill Wolf's poem. Which statement best explains what the speaker means by using her 'heart' to see?

options.label: A
options.text: The speaker believes her heart is stronger and more reliable than her eyes.

options.label: B
options.text: The speaker feels that her friends hide their true selves and she must search for them.

options.label: C
options.text: The speaker is describing a physical act of looking very carefully at her friends.

options.label: D
options.text: The speaker wants to understand her friends through empathy and feeling, not just outward observation.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Suggests the student read the line literally rather than recognising the heart as an image of empathy.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Indicates a confusion between the metaphorical and literal registers of the poem.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Introduces a mistrust or concealment idea not present in the poem's warm, accepting tone.

items.source_lo: Student identifies and interprets the speaker's feelings, intentions, and values using a lyric poem as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Selfless devotion, unconditional acceptance, empathy as basis of friendship; AABB prayer-cadence poem by Jill Wolf.
items.item_stem: In the poem, the speaker says she will "make no judgements from afar" and will "love my friends the way they are." What do these two lines together reveal about the speaker's idea of what a true friend should be? Support your answer with a detail from the poem.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The two lines show that the speaker believes a true friend accepts others without criticism or conditions, loving them as they are rather than judging them from a distance. This is reinforced by her earlier wish to actively make her friends' wishes come true, showing that acceptance is paired with active care.

items.source_lo: Student recalls and identifies specific details from a listened-to spoken text using a short informational talk as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Outdoor activities of two friends Ajay and Dhiraj: swings, slides, park walks, birdwatching, cycling, ice-cream, comic-book reading.
items.item_stem: Your teacher will read a short talk about what two friends, Ajay and Dhiraj, enjoy doing together. Listen carefully. Which of the following statements about Ajay and Dhiraj are true?

options.text: Ajay enjoys the slides the most when they visit the park.
Both friends enjoy eating ice-cream together.
Dhiraj and Ajay go cycling every Sunday morning.
They sit on a park bench and read a comic book together.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer:
1. True — the transcript states Ajay enjoys slides the most.
2. False — the transcript says they go cycling on Saturdays, not Sundays.
3. True — the transcript states that what both truly enjoy is eating ice-cream together.
4. True — the transcript states they purchase a comic book, sit on a park bench and read together.

items.source_lo: Student recalls and identifies specific details from a listened-to spoken text using a short informational talk as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Outdoor activities of two friends Ajay and Dhiraj: swings, slides, park walks, birdwatching, cycling, ice-cream, comic-book reading.
items.item_stem: Your teacher will read the talk about Ajay and Dhiraj again. Listen and then answer: What does the talk tell us about why Dhiraj enjoys walks in the park? Give two details from what you heard.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Dhiraj likes nature, and during their park walks both friends listen to birds and look at the trees. These two details — his love of nature and the activities of birdwatching and tree-watching — explain why he enjoys the walks.

items.item_stem: Work with a partner. One of you is Friend A, the other is Friend B. Friend A greets Friend B and invites them to come to the park. Friend B is not free but suggests another activity you can do together. Carry on the conversation: plan what you will do, say what you enjoy about spending time together, and end by thanking each other.

expected_elements: Greets the partner naturally and issues a clear invitation.
Responds to refusal and proposes an alternative activity.
States what they enjoy about time spent together.
Uses appropriate expressions of appreciation and thanks to close.

items.item_stem: You and your partner are friends at school during the lunch break. Your partner notices you look upset. Take turns to play the friend who is upset and the friend who tries to help. The helping friend should ask what is wrong, listen carefully, offer one suggestion, and say something kind. The upset friend should explain the problem and respond to the suggestion. Share your opinion: do you think the kind words helped? Why?

expected_elements: Shows empathy by asking and listening before advising.
Offers a specific, relevant suggestion rather than a vague one.
Uses kind, supportive language to express care.
Gives a brief, reasoned opinion on whether the words helped.

items.item_stem: Before you write, fill in the planning table below. Then use your notes to write a short paragraph of about 60 words describing your first day at your current school. Give your paragraph a title.
items.visual_stimulus:
| Planning question | Your answer |
| When did you arrive at school for the first time? | |
| Where did you go first? | |
| How did you feel? | |

expected_elements: Fills in all three planning prompts before writing.
Paragraph has a clear title and stays close to about 60 words.
Uses complete sentences drawn from the planning notes.
Includes at least one detail about a feeling or person met.

items.item_stem: The speaker in the poem says she wants to make her friends' wishes come true. Think of a time when you did something kind for a friend, or a friend did something kind for you, without being asked. Write a paragraph of about 80 words describing what happened, how it made the other person feel, and what it taught you about friendship. Give your paragraph a title of your own.

expected_elements: Describes a specific act of kindness, not a general statement.
Includes how the other person felt as a result.
States clearly what the writer learned about friendship.
Paragraph has a suitable title and is approximately 80 words.

items.source_context: Synonyms for 'blessed'; friendship-quality words loyal, helpful, kind, caring, honest used in fill-in sentences.
items.item_stem: Match each friendship-quality word from Column A with its closest meaning from Column B.
items.visual_stimulus:
| Column A | Column B |
| loyal | always telling the truth |
| honest | showing kindness and concern for others |
| caring | faithful and supportive no matter what |
| kind | not lying or cheating |
| helpful | willing to do things for others |

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: loyal – faithful and supportive no matter what; honest – always telling the truth; caring – showing kindness and concern for others; kind – not lying or cheating; helpful – willing to do things for others.

answer_key.right: faithful and supportive no matter what
showing kindness and concern for others
willing to do things for others

items.source_context: Synonyms for 'blessed'; friendship-quality words loyal, helpful, kind, caring, honest used in fill-in sentences.
items.item_stem: The poem says the speaker feels 'blessed' to have special friends. The word 'blessed' can mean feeling grateful, fortunate, and deeply valued. Choose TWO of the following friendship-quality words — loyal, caring, honest — and write one sentence for each, showing clearly what the word means through a situation between two friends.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Accept any two sentences that demonstrate accurate understanding of the chosen words through a plausible friendship situation; for example, 'My friend Priya is loyal because she stayed by my side when the other children laughed at me' or 'My friend is honest — he told me kindly that my drawing had a mistake so I could fix it.'

items.item_stem:
Read the two friendship quotations below and answer the questions that follow.

(i) 'A friend in need is a friend indeed.'
(ii) 'My best friend is the one who brings out the best in me.'

1. In your own words, explain what quotation (i) means.
2. Which of the two quotations do you think fits the speaker in the poem 'A Friend's Prayer' better? Give one reason for your choice.

expected_elements: Explains quotation (i) as meaning a true friend helps when you are in trouble.
Makes a clear choice between the two quotations with a reason.
Links the chosen quotation to a specific value or action in the poem.
Uses own words; does not copy the quotation as the explanation.

items.source_context: Two friendship quotations — 'A friend in need is a friend indeed' and 'My best friend is the one who brings out the best in me' — plus a decorated quotation for the class board.
items.item_stem: Find or compose ONE quotation about friendship — it may be in English or in your own language (write an English translation if it is in another language). On a sheet of paper, write the quotation neatly, colour and decorate it, and write two to three sentences below it explaining: (a) what the quotation means to you, and (b) one experience from your own life that this quotation reminds you of.

expected_elements: Quotation is clearly written and attributed if a known source exists.
Decoration is neat and the overall presentation is readable.
Explanation shows genuine personal understanding of the quotation's meaning.
Personal experience described is specific and connected to the quotation.
